# Phase 1: Data Understanding and Exploratory Analysis

## Background and data source

The dataset is derived from Salam & El Hibaoui, *Power Consumption of
Tetouan City* (UCI Machine Learning Repository). The original data
record the active power consumed every 10 minutes by the three
distribution zones of Tetouan (Morocco) during 2017.

For each (day $d$, hour $h$) pair we define the **hourly load factor**:

$$
\mathrm{LF}(d, h) = \frac{\overline{P}(d, h)}{\max_{h'} \overline{P}(d, h')}
$$

where
$\overline{P}(d,h) = \text{Zone1}(d,h) + \text{Zone2}(d,h) + \text{Zone3}(d,h)$
is the city-wide hourly mean power. By construction
$\mathrm{LF}(d,h) \in [0, 1]$: the daily peak hour equals exactly 1,
while the deepest off-peak hour yields the smallest value.

From the full $365 \times 24 \approx 8700$ cells a uniform random
subsample of **2000 rows** was drawn. Values are clamped to
$(10^{-3},\, 1 - 10^{-3})$ so that the **Beta log-density is finite at
the boundaries** — a requirement for Bayesian inference with Stan.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Loading and initial inspection

```{r load-data}
lf <- read.csv("hourly_load_factor.csv")

# Parse dates and add temporal variables
lf$date   <- mdy(lf$date)
lf$month  <- month(lf$date)
lf$season <- cut(lf$month,
                 breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12),
                 labels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Autumn"),
                 include.lowest = FALSE)

cat("Dimensions:", nrow(lf), "rows x", ncol(lf), "columns\n")
head(lf)

```

```{r check-na}
cat("Missing values:", sum(is.na(lf$load_factor)), "\n")
cat("load_factor range: [", min(lf$load_factor), ",", max(lf$load_factor), "]\n")
cat("Unique hours:", length(unique(lf$hour)), " (from", min(lf$hour), "to", max(lf$hour), ")\n")
```

The dataset is complete: 2000 rows, no NA values, `load_factor` strictly
inside $(10^{-3}, 1 - 10^{-3})$, `hour` in $\{0, \ldots, 23\}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Descriptive statistics

```{r summary-stats}
lf |>
  summarise(
    n      = n(),
    min    = round(min(load_factor), 4),
    q1     = round(quantile(load_factor, 0.25), 4),
    median = round(median(load_factor), 4),
    mean   = round(mean(load_factor), 4),
    q3     = round(quantile(load_factor, 0.75), 4),
    max    = round(max(load_factor), 4),
    sd     = round(sd(load_factor), 4)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Descriptive statistics of the load factor (n = 2000)")
```

The distribution is left-skewed (median \> mean), with the lower tail
corresponding to nighttime off-peak hours. The effective range
(\~0.43–0.999) is wide, indicating that at peak hours the load factor
reaches the upper clamping boundary.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Plot 1 — Overall histogram with kernel density

```{r hist-global, fig.cap="Empirical density of the load factor (n = 2000). The orange curve is the kernel density estimate."}
hist(lf$load_factor, breaks = 35, freq = FALSE,
     col = "tomato", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor (hourly load / daily peak)",
     main = "Hourly city load factor — empirical density (n = 2000)")
lines(density(lf$load_factor, from = 0.001, to = 0.999),
      col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
```

The histogram reveals a **clearly trimodal** distribution:

-   **Lower mode** (around LF ≈ 0.52–0.55): deep off-peak hours
    (pre-dawn), when consumption is far below the daily peak.
-   **Middle mode** (around LF ≈ 0.72–0.75): daytime hours, when
    consumption reaches a moderate plateau.
-   **Upper spike** near LF ≈ 0.999: the peak-hour observations, which
    by construction sit at the daily maximum before clamping. This is a
    distinct third concentration, not a tail.

This trimodality motivates the use of a **Beta mixture model** (Phase 2)
rather than a single Beta distribution, and suggests $H = 3$ components
as a plausible starting point.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Plot 2 — Boxplot of load factor by hour of the day

```{r boxplot-hour, fig.cap="Load factor distribution by hour. True off-peak valley at hours 4-7; evening peak (hours 19-21) dominates over midday plateau (hours 11-16)."}


ggplot(lf, aes(x = factor(hour), y = load_factor)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x     = "Hour of the day",
    y     = "Load factor",
    title = "Load factor distribution by hour"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))
```

The daily pattern is clear:

-   **Late night / early morning** (hours 0–3): moderate medians
    (\~0.62–0.68) — these are not the lowest hours; the city still
    consumes a significant fraction of its peak load.
-   **Deep off-peak valley** (hours 4–7): the true minimum, with medians
    \~0.52–0.53 and tight IQRs — all days converge to very low
    consumption before dawn.
-   **Midday plateau** (hours 11–16): medians rise to \~0.73–0.77,
    forming a broad flat shoulder in the daily profile.
-   **Dominant evening peak** (hours 19–21): medians jump to
    \~0.90–0.97, clearly the highest window of the day. Hour 18 also
    shows exceptional spread (IQR spanning almost 0.70–0.97), reflecting
    the sharp onset of the evening load surge.
-   The trimodal histogram arises from the superposition of these three
    regimes (off-peak / midday plateau / evening peak).

This hourly pattern will reappear in **Phase 3** (MAP component
assignment as a function of hour) and **Phase 4** (multinomial logistic
regression with Fourier-transformed hour as covariate).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Plot 3 — Density ridgeline by hour

```{r ridgeline, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Load factor density for each of the 24 hours. Colour encodes the LF value."}
ggplot(lf, aes(x = load_factor, y = factor(hour), fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(scale = 1.8, rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "LF", option = "C") +
  labs(
    x     = "Load factor",
    y     = "Hour of the day",
    title = "Load factor density by hour of the day"
  ) +
  theme_ridges(grid = TRUE)
```

The ridgeline plot shows how the **shape of the distribution changes
with the hour**:

-   **Hours 4–7**: the true off-peak block — very narrow, left-shifted
    peaks concentrated at LF ≈ 0.52–0.55 with almost no spread. These
    are the most homogeneous hours.
-   **Hours 0–3**: moderate LF but with long right tails extending
    towards 1.0, indicating that on some days (summer peak-demand
    evenings running past midnight) these hours can still carry
    near-peak load. The distributions are bimodal or skewed.
-   **Hours 8–10**: broad transition distributions, reflecting the
    morning ramp-up.
-   **Hours 11–16**: fairly concentrated peaks at LF ≈ 0.73–0.77,
    forming the midday plateau.
-   **Hours 19–21**: extremely narrow, right-concentrated peaks near LF
    ≈ 0.95–0.99 — the sharpest and most consistent regime in the
    dataset, corresponding to the evening peak.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Plot 4 — Mean load factor heatmap (hour x month)

```{r heatmap, fig.cap="Mean load factor by hour and month. Summer months (June-August) show higher consumption in afternoon hours (air conditioning peak)."}
lf |>
  group_by(hour, month) |>
  summarise(mean_lf = mean(load_factor), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = hour, fill = mean_lf)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "B", name = "Mean LF") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12,
                     labels = c("Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun",
                                "Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean load factor — hour x month",
    x     = "Month",
    y     = "Hour of the day"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The heatmap highlights two effects:

-   **Daily cycle (dominant)**: the horizontal banding is the strongest
    signal — a dark band at hours 4–7 (deep off-peak, near LF ≈ 0.50)
    and a bright yellow-white band at hours 19–22 (evening peak, near LF
    ≈ 0.90+) run consistently across all 12 months.
-   **Seasonal modulation (subtle)**: there is a mild brightening of the
    afternoon block (hours 12–17) in summer months (Jun–Aug), consistent
    with air-conditioning demand in Tetouan's hot Mediterranean climate.
    However, the effect is modest compared to the daily cycle. A notable
    anomalous warm cell appears in June at hours 0–2, likely a sampling
    artifact from the 2000-row subsample rather than a genuine physical
    pattern.

The Fourier-transformed hour covariates used in **Phase 4** are designed
to capture exactly the 24-hour periodicity — the dominant structure
visible here.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Assessment of the single Beta approximation

```{r fit-beta, fig.cap="MLE diagnostics for a single Beta fit. Systematic deviations in the QQ-plot motivate the mixture model."}
fit_beta <- fitdist(lf$load_factor, "beta")
cat("MLE parameters: alpha =", round(fit_beta$estimate["shape1"], 3),
    "| beta =", round(fit_beta$estimate["shape2"], 3), "\n")
plot(fit_beta)
```

```{r beta-overlay, fig.cap="Empirical density vs. single Beta MLE. The single Beta cannot replicate the bimodality."}
hist(lf$load_factor, breaks = 35, freq = FALSE,
     col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlab = "Load factor",
     main = "Empirical density vs. single Beta MLE")
x_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)
lines(x_seq,
      dbeta(x_seq, fit_beta$estimate["shape1"], fit_beta$estimate["shape2"]),
      col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
lines(density(lf$load_factor, from = 0.001, to = 0.999),
      col = "darkorange", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Kernel density", "Single Beta MLE"),
       col    = c("darkorange", "firebrick"),
       lty    = c(2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The single Beta fit is dramatically inadequate. The MLE curve is
**monotonically increasing** (J-shaped), concentrating density near LF =
1 — the optimizer trades off the lower modes entirely to accommodate the
strong spike near 0.999. The empirical data, in contrast, shows three
distinct concentrations. The QQ and PP plots confirm systematic
deviation across the entire support. A single Beta cannot produce
multiple peaks regardless of its parameters: with
$\alpha > 1, \beta > 1$ it is bell-shaped; with $\beta < 1$ it is
J-shaped (as here); neither can match a trimodal distribution. This
motivates a **Beta mixture** with $H \geq 3$ components in Phase 2.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Phase 1 summary

| Aspect | Finding |
|----|----|
| Overall distribution | Trimodal: off-peak \~0.52–0.55, midday plateau \~0.72–0.75, evening spike \~0.999 |
| Hourly pattern | Valley hours 4–7; hours 0–3 moderate; midday plateau 11–16; evening peak 19–21 |
| Seasonality | Daily cycle dominates; mild summer afternoon enhancement; anomaly in June hours 0–2 |
| Single Beta fit | Fails dramatically: MLE yields a J-shaped curve, misses all three modes |
| Mixture motivation | H = 3 components expected optimal (to be confirmed via WAIC in Phase 2) |

The structure identified here directly informs the modelling choices in
subsequent phases:

-   **Phase 2**: Beta mixture with $H \in \{1,\ldots,5\}$, model
    selection via WAIC
-   **Phase 3**: MAP assignment — mixture components correspond to
    hourly regimes (off-peak / peak)
-   **Phase 4**: multinomial logistic regression with covariates
    $\sin(k \cdot 2\pi h / 24)$, $\cos(k \cdot 2\pi h / 24)$ to capture
    the daily periodicity

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Phase 2: Beta mixture with $H \in \{1,\ldots,5\}$, model selection via WAIC

```{r, eval=FALSE}
cat("Estimate for the single beta model (H=1)...\n")

fit_h1 <- brm(
  formula = load_factor ~ 1,       
  family = Beta(),                 
  data = lf,
  chains = 4,                       
  iter = 2000,                      
  seed = 42                       
)
fit_h1 <- add_criterion(fit_h1, "waic")

fit_h2 <- brm(
  formula = load_factor ~ 1,
  family = mixture(Beta, nmix = 2),
  data = lf,
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 42
)
fit_h2 <- add_criterion(fit_h2, "waic")

fit_h3 <- brm(
  formula = load_factor ~ 1,
  family = mixture(Beta, nmix = 3),
  data = lf,
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 42
)
fit_h3 <- add_criterion(fit_h3, "waic")

fit_h4 <- brm(
  formula = load_factor ~ 1,
  family = mixture(Beta, nmix = 4),
  data = lf,
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 42
)
fit_h4 <- add_criterion(fit_h4, "waic")

fit_h5 <- brm(
  formula = load_factor ~ 1,
  family = mixture(Beta, nmix = 5),
  data = lf,
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, seed = 42
)
fit_h5 <- add_criterion(fit_h5, "waic")
```

```{r}
fit_h1 <- readRDS("modello_H1.rds")
fit_h2 <- readRDS("modello_H2.rds")
fit_h3 <- readRDS("modello_H3.rds")
fit_h4 <- readRDS("modello_H4.rds")
fit_h5 <- readRDS("modello_H5.rds")

model_comparison <- loo_compare(fit_h1, fit_h2, fit_h3, fit_h4, fit_h5, criterion = "waic")
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(model_comparison), digits = 2, caption = "WAIC Comparison across Mixture Models")
```

```{r}
library(brms)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

fit_h1 <- readRDS("modello_H1.rds")
fit_h3 <- readRDS("modello_H3.rds")
fit_h5 <- readRDS("modello_H5.rds")

p1 <- pp_check(fit_h1, ndraws = 100) + labs(title = "Model H=1 (Single Beta)")
p3 <- pp_check(fit_h3, ndraws = 100) + labs(title = "Model H=3 (Mixture)")
p5 <- pp_check(fit_h5, ndraws = 100) + labs(title = "Model H=5 (Mixture)")

grid.arrange(p1, p3, p5, ncol = 1)
```

Model selection using the WAIC criterion yielded a counterintuitive
result compared to pure visual inspection. Although the empirical
histogram suggests a trimodal structure ($H=3$), the 5-component mixture
model ($H=5$) proves to be vastly superior, showing a highly significant
predictive difference (elpd_diff = -50.2) compared to the $H=4$ model
(se_diff = 6.3).This discrepancy suggests that the individual peaks
(modes) present in the data possess complex asymmetry or tail behavior
that a single Beta distribution cannot adequately parameterize.
Consequently, the Bayesian process utilizes the additional mixture
components not to identify new, isolated data clusters, but rather to
correct and refine the shape of the individual empirical distributions.
This ensures a significantly superior fit, ultimately justifying the
penalty introduced by the WAIC for the higher parametric complexity.
